When Natasha came out of the drawing room and ran off, she got only as far as the flower room. There she stopped, listening to the voices in the drawing room and waiting for Boris to come out. She was already beginning to grow impatient and, stamping her little foot, was just about to cry because he had not come at once, when she heard the measured footsteps of a young man, neither quiet nor hurried. Natasha quickly darted between the tubs of flowers and hid.

Boris stopped in the middle of the room, looked around, brushed specks from the sleeve of his uniform with his hand, and went up to the mirror, examining his handsome face. Natasha, keeping very quiet, peered out from her hiding place, waiting to see what he would do. He stood before the mirror for a while, smiled, and went toward the door leading out. Natasha wanted to call to him, but then thought better of it.

“Let him look for me,” she said to herself. No sooner had Boris gone out than a flushed Sonya emerged from another door, angrily whispering something through her tears. Natasha restrained her first impulse to run out to her and remained in her hiding place, as though under a cap of invisibility, watching to see what was happening in the world. She was experiencing a peculiar new delight. Sonya was whispering something and looking back at the drawing-room door. Nikolai came out through the door.

“Sonya! What is the matter with you? How can you behave like this?” said Nikolai, running up to her.

“Nothing, nothing; leave me alone!” Sonya burst into sobs.

“No, I know what it is.”

“Well, if you know, so much the better; go to her.”

“Sooonya! Just one word! How can you torment both me and yourself over a fancy?” Nikolai said, taking her hand.

Sonya did not pull her hand away from him and stopped crying.

Without moving or breathing, Natasha watched from her hiding place with shining eyes. “What will happen now?” she thought.

“Sonya! I do not need the whole world! You alone are everything to me,” Nikolai said. “I will prove it to you.”

“I do not like it when you talk like that.”

“Very well, I won’t; forgive me, Sonya!” He drew her to him and kissed her.

“Oh, how wonderful!” Natasha thought, and when Sonya and Nikolai had left the room, she followed them and summoned Boris to her.

“Boris, come here,” she said with a significant and sly expression. “I need to tell you one thing. Here, here,” she said, and led him into the flower room, to the place between the tubs where she had been hiding. Boris followed her, smiling.

“And what is this one thing?” he asked.

She became embarrassed, looked around, and, seeing her doll lying on one of the tubs, picked it up.

“Kiss the doll,” she said.

Boris looked intently and tenderly at her animated face and did not answer.

“You don’t want to? Well then, come here,” she said, moving farther in among the flowers and throwing down the doll. “Closer, closer!” she whispered. She caught the officer by his cuffs with both hands, and solemnity and fear were visible in her flushed face.

“Would you like to kiss me?” she whispered, barely audibly, looking up at him from under her brows, smiling and almost crying with excitement.

Boris blushed.

“How funny you are!” he said, bending down toward her, blushing still more, but doing nothing and waiting.

She suddenly jumped onto a tub, so that she stood higher than he did, put both arms around him, so that her slender bare arms bent above his neck, and, tossing her hair back with a movement of her head, kissed him full on the lips.

She slipped between the pots to the other side of the flowers and stopped, lowering her head.

“Natasha,” he said, “you know that I love you, but...”

“You are in love with me?” Natasha interrupted him.

“Yes, I am in love, but please, let us not do what we just... Four more years... Then I will ask for your hand.”

Natasha thought.

“Thirteen, fourteen, fifteen, sixteen...” she said, counting on her slender little fingers. “All right! Then it is settled?”

And a smile of joy and relief lit up her animated face.

“It is settled!” said Boris.

“Forever?” said the girl. “Until death itself?”

And, taking his arm, she walked quietly beside him into the sofa room with a happy face.

XI.

The countess was so tired from receiving visitors that she gave orders not to admit anyone else, and the porter was instructed merely to be sure to invite to dinner anyone else who might arrive with congratulations. The countess wanted to speak in private with her childhood friend, Princess Anna Mikhailovna, whom she had not had a proper chance to see since her arrival from Petersburg. Anna Mikhailovna, her tear-stained face still pleasant, moved closer to the countess’s armchair.

“With you I shall be completely frank,” said Anna Mikhailovna. “So few of us old friends are left! That is why I value your friendship so highly.”

Anna Mikhailovna looked at Vera and stopped. The countess pressed her friend’s hand.

“Vera,” said the countess, addressing her eldest daughter, who was plainly unloved. “How can you have no understanding of anything? Can’t you feel that you are not wanted here? Go to your sisters, or...”

The beautiful Vera smiled disdainfully, evidently without feeling the slightest offense.

“If you had told me sooner, Mamma, I would have left at once,” she said, and went to her room.

But as she passed the sofa room, she noticed two couples sitting symmetrically by its two windows. She stopped and smiled disdainfully. Sonya sat close beside Nikolai, who was copying out for her some verses he had composed for the first time. Boris and Natasha were sitting by the other window and fell silent when Vera entered. Sonya and Natasha looked at Vera with guilty and happy faces.

It was delightful and touching to look at these girls in love, but the sight of them evidently aroused no pleasant feeling in Vera.

“How many times have I asked you,” she said, “not to take my things? You have a room of your own.” She took the inkwell from Nikolai.

“At once, at once,” he said, dipping his pen.

“You always manage to do everything at the wrong time,” said Vera. “You came running into the drawing room like that, so that everyone was ashamed of you.”

Although—or precisely because—what she had said was perfectly just, no one answered her, and all four merely exchanged glances. She lingered in the room with the inkwell in her hand.

“And what secrets can there possibly be at your age between Natasha and Boris, and between you two? Nothing but foolishness!”

“Well, what business is it of yours, Vera?” Natasha said softly, coming to their defense.

That day she was evidently even kinder and more affectionate toward everyone than usual.

“Very foolish,” said Vera. “I am ashamed of you. What sort of secrets are they?”

“Everyone has their own secrets. We do not interfere with you and Berg,” Natasha said, growing heated.

“I should think you do not,” said Vera, “because there can never be anything improper in my conduct.
